source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

stimulus.text:
Share of all immigrants to the United States, by country of birth (percent).

| Country | 1861–1870 | 1891–1900 |
| Great Britain | 24.5 | 7.5 |
| Ireland | 18.8 | 10.0 |
| Germany | 34.0 | 14.0 |
| Austria-Hungary | 0.3 | 16.0 |
| Russia and Poland | 0.2 | 14.0 |
| Italy | 0.5 | 18.0 |
stimulus.source_note: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), article “Migration,” table of nationality of immigrants, compiled from official United States immigration figures. Public domain.

stem: A nativist in the 1890s could have used this table to argue that

options.text: immigration had ended because the old sources had dried up
options.misconception: Reads falling old shares as an ending, ignoring the rising new shares.

options.text: the new immigrants came from the same countries as before
options.misconception: Claims the same origins, but the table shows the sources changing.

options.text: the newcomers were increasingly unlike the earlier immigrants in origin
the British share proved that America was still British
options.misconception: Reads a falling British share as proof of British America.

rationales.A: The old sources fell, but the new sources rose past them. Immigration did not end; its origins changed.
rationales.B: The table shows the opposite: the largest shares moved from Britain, Ireland, and Germany to Italy, Austria-Hungary, and Russia and Poland.
rationales.C: The table shows the largest shares moving from Germany, Britain, and Ireland to Italy, Austria-Hungary, and Russia and Poland. A nativist could point to that shift as proof that the newcomers were unlike the earlier immigrants.
rationales.D: The British share falls from 24.5 to 7.5. The table shows Britain fading, not America staying British.
rationales.general:
Read the table the way a nativist would have read it.
1. In 1861-1870 the largest shares came from Germany, Britain, and Ireland.
2. By 1891-1900 the largest shares came from Italy, Austria-Hungary, and Russia and Poland.
3. Background from the books: nativists judged the new immigrants unlike earlier Americans in language and custom.
4. So the table hands the nativist a picture of newcomers unlike the old ones.
Remember: a table argues when its shift matches the fear it is used to feed.
